doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Dexter Gordon: power, laid-back phrasing and sound versus Getz
summary: Four years in Gordon's quartet with Eddie Gladden and George Cables, and Gordon's behind-the-beat phrasing even when not drinking.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: Well said. Let me run a couple of names by you and see if they strike you as, what did you learn from them or learn not to do, or anything in particular. Dexter Gordon?

Wow. Powerful. Imposing. He was an imposing figure when he played it was huge. All his ideas were incredibly clear. And so I had to be clear with him at all times. And he wanted it to be powerful under him as a unit. So I had to really be strong and Eddie Gladden and I had to really work well together, and when George came in we were one. He demanded it the way he played. And when you heard it, then it became the quartet. Not four people playing at the same time, or Dexter playing and the trio was playing behind him. It was the sound of the quartet. I still reap the benefits of having been part of that group for four solid years. At that time we were traveling maybe eight months out of the year. Pretty intense. And to me, between he, Eddie Harris before he, really working, Thad Jones/Mel Lewis, two years with them, and then four years, that’s really how I learned how to play, I mean really play. You didn’t have a choice if you wanted to stay there.
Dexter always seemed like he was a master at playing behind the beat it seemed to me.

Well that was his — a lot of people thought that’s the way he played because he drank a lot. But that’s not it. He heard that. That’s the way he played. He kind of was laid back. Because I played with him when he wasn’t drinking at all. And he still played the same

way. And some people don’t really believe that, but it’s really true. He just heard that, the way that he phrased. And you can’t write it, you can’t transpose it, you just have to say, “Well just play this laid back.” Well what does that mean? But he was really consistent at that. So he heard that. That wasn’t something that — and the sound. It was just a full- bodied sound. I mean I’ve had a career with tenor players. And he was on the bottom. I mean he had this huge sound. And Stan Getz flipped it. They’re almost the same age too. But Stan’s voice was more in the mid-range and upper. And every once in a while he went down. But it was really interesting to me.
